items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Use of plain nonmedical language during patient education
items.mechanism: Plain language reduces unnecessary cognitive and vocabulary burden. Medical terms should be avoided when a simpler accurate alternative exists; when a necessary medical term is introduced, it should be defined in understandable language.
items.vignette: A 63-year-old man with newly diagnosed chronic kidney disease says that he is confused by the terms used during previous visits. His physician wants to explain why his kidney function will be monitored with repeat blood and urine testing.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to explain the plan?

options.A: Use standard nephrology terminology so the patient becomes accustomed to the language used in medical records
options.B: Give the patient a detailed written glossary of renal physiology before discussing the testing plan
options.C: Explain the plan using common words, define any necessary medical term, and give specific concrete instructions
options.D: Avoid discussing the testing details and tell the patient that the laboratory will know which studies to obtain
options.E: Speak more slowly while using the same technical terminology used in the prior visits

items.key_expl: AHRQ recommends plain, nonmedical language and specific, concrete explanations. Necessary medical terms should be defined rather than used as unexplained jargon.

distractor_notes.A: Routine use of unexplained technical vocabulary does not follow clear-communication guidance.
distractor_notes.B: A glossary does not substitute for a clear verbal explanation of the immediate plan and may add unnecessary information burden.
distractor_notes.D: Withholding information prevents patient understanding and participation.
distractor_notes.E: Slowing speech does not make unexplained jargon understandable.

items.objective: Use plain, nonmedical language and concrete instructions when explaining medical information, defining necessary technical terms in understandable words.

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Using open-ended wording to invite patient questions
items.mechanism: Open-ended invitations normalize questions and communicate that the clinician expects and has time for them. A yes/no question such as 'Do you have any questions?' is less effective because patients commonly answer no despite unresolved concerns.
items.vignette: After explaining a new diagnosis and treatment plan, a physician notices that a patient remains quiet and repeatedly looks at the printed instructions. The physician wants to make it easier for the patient to raise unresolved concerns.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next statement?

options.A: ‘We covered a lot. What questions can I answer for you?’
options.C: ‘Everything should be clear from the handout, correct?’
options.D: ‘You can call the office later if you discover that something was unclear.’
options.E: ‘Before we finish, please tell me that you understand the plan.’

items.key_expl: AHRQ specifically recommends open-ended invitations such as 'What questions can I answer for you?' and advises against relying on 'Do you have any questions?' because patients often respond no even when they have questions.

distractor_notes.B: The yes/no format is specifically discouraged as a sole invitation for questions.
distractor_notes.C: This is leading and discourages disclosure of confusion.
distractor_notes.D: Deferring questions misses the opportunity to identify concerns during the encounter.
distractor_notes.E: Requesting an assertion of understanding does not invite the patient's actual questions.

items.objective: Invite patient questions with open-ended, normalizing wording rather than a yes/no question that implicitly favors a negative response.

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Opening the interview with an open-ended question and listening without interruption
items.mechanism: Open-ended questions allow patients to voice concerns in their own words and active listening without premature interruption supports information gathering before the clinician narrows the interview with focused questions.
items.vignette: A 37-year-old woman comes for a first visit after several months of fatigue and poor sleep. The referral note lists possible anxiety, but the physician has not yet heard the patient's account of what has been happening.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to begin the interview?

options.A: Ask a rapid series of yes-or-no questions about anxiety, depressed mood, and insomnia
options.B: Begin by explaining that the referral suggests anxiety and ask whether she agrees
options.C: Ask her to rank her symptoms from most to least important before she describes them
options.D: Review the referral note aloud and correct any details that appear inconsistent
options.E: Ask what has been bothering her most and allow her to describe her concerns without interruption before moving to focused questions

items.key_expl: AHRQ recommends open-ended questions to encourage participation and listening without interruption. This allows the patient's perspective to emerge before the clinician imposes a diagnostic frame or narrows the history.

distractor_notes.A: Closed questions can be useful later but are a poor opening when the patient's account has not yet been elicited.
distractor_notes.B: Leading with the referral diagnosis risks framing the patient's narrative before hearing it.
distractor_notes.C: Ranking symptoms before hearing the narrative constrains information gathering prematurely.
distractor_notes.D: The referral note should not substitute for the patient's own history.

items.objective: Begin patient-centered information gathering with an open-ended invitation and active listening before transitioning to focused questions.
duplicate_probe_terms: listen without interrupting open-ended questions patient concerns

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Proactively eliciting medication cost as a barrier to adherence
items.mechanism: Patients may delay, ration, or not obtain medication because of cost and may feel embarrassed to volunteer the problem. Clinicians should normalize and directly ask about cost burden, then work with the patient and care team on feasible alternatives or assistance.
items.vignette: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension has had poor blood pressure control despite repeated prescriptions. Pharmacy refill data show long gaps between refills. She says, ‘I know the medicine is important, but sometimes I have to make it last until the next paycheck.’
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next response?

options.A: Warn her that continued nonadherence may lead the clinic to stop prescribing medication
options.B: Increase the dose because refill gaps suggest that the current regimen is ineffective
options.C: Ask her to sign a statement promising to take every dose as prescribed
options.D: Ask whether medication cost is a burden, explore what she has been doing to make it last, and discuss lower-cost or assistance options
options.E: Tell her to prioritize medicine over nonmedical household expenses without asking for additional details

items.key_expl: AHRQ recommends directly and sensitively asking whether medication cost is a burden, including whether patients delay or take less medication to make it last, and helping them access affordable options or financial assistance.

distractor_notes.A: Punitive language does not identify or address the cost barrier.
distractor_notes.B: The problem is medication access and rationing, not evidence that the prescribed dose is pharmacologically inadequate.
distractor_notes.C: A promise does not remove a financial barrier.
distractor_notes.E: Judgmental financial advice bypasses assessment of the patient's actual constraints and available assistance.

items.objective: Recognize and address cost-related medication nonadherence by asking directly and nonjudgmentally about affordability and connecting the patient with feasible lower-cost or assistance options.

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Eliciting transportation and other social barriers before labeling a patient nonadherent
items.mechanism: Food, housing, transportation, work, childcare, and other social needs can prevent patients from following care plans. Identifying these barriers permits counseling, referral, and shared selection of a treatment plan that is feasible for the patient.
items.vignette: A 48-year-old man with diabetes has missed three specialty appointments and is described in the referral note as ‘noncompliant.’ When asked about the missed visits, he says that he recently lost access to a car and the specialty clinic is two bus transfers from his home. He also cannot miss another shift at work this month.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Document that he is unwilling to participate in care because he has missed multiple appointments
options.B: Acknowledge the transportation and work barriers, assess what alternatives are feasible, and connect him with available scheduling or community support resources
options.C: Explain that medical appointments must take priority over employment obligations
options.D: Ask a family member to take responsibility for transporting him to all future appointments
options.E: Discharge him from the specialty referral pathway until he demonstrates better attendance

items.key_expl: AHRQ identifies transportation and related social needs as barriers that should be assessed and addressed through counseling, assistance, referral, and treatment planning rather than interpreted automatically as unwillingness to participate in care.

distractor_notes.A: The patient has stated concrete access barriers; labeling him unwilling ignores the information provided.
distractor_notes.C: A directive that ignores employment constraints does not make the care plan feasible.
distractor_notes.D: Family help may be useful if the patient wants it, but assigning responsibility to a family member without first assessing feasible options is not the best next step.
distractor_notes.E: Removing access worsens the identified barrier rather than addressing it.

items.objective: When apparent nonadherence reflects social barriers, identify the specific barrier and collaboratively connect the patient with feasible support and care alternatives.
